title: Charging for the road
bodyMd:
When a city puts a price on driving into its centre, the first effect is easy to measure and the second is not. Valdera, a northern European city of 900,000 people, introduced a daily charge of 8 euros for entering its inner ring in March 2021. Traffic crossing the cordon fell by 17 per cent within a year, and average bus speeds inside the ring rose from 11 to 14 kilometres an hour. Those are the headline numbers, and they are the ones that travel.

The harder question is who pays. A flat daily charge takes the same 8 euros from a lawyer driving a saloon and from a night-shift cleaner whose bus route was withdrawn in 2019, and as a share of income the second payment is far heavier. Valdera's council answered the objection by earmarking the revenue: of the 61 million euros collected in the first full year, 44 million went to extending two tram lines and the remainder funded an exemption scheme for residents living inside the cordon. Critics noted that the exemption benefited the wealthiest district in the city, and that the tram extensions were not due to open until 2026, so for five years the burden would fall before the compensation arrived.

Economists who study road pricing tend to make a narrower claim than either side in that argument. Their point is that an untolled road is not free; it is paid for in time, and time is distributed as unequally as money. A congestion charge converts a queue into a price, and a price, unlike a queue, can be handed back to whoever the city chooses. Whether it is handed back well is a political question rather than an economic one, which is why the design of the exemptions, rather than the level of the charge, is where most schemes succeed or fail.
accessibilityText: A three-paragraph prose passage about urban congestion charging, set in a fictional northern European city called Valdera. There is no table, figure or mathematical notation. The passage states these figures in words: Valdera has 900,000 people; the daily charge to enter the inner ring is 8 euros and began in March 2021; traffic crossing the cordon fell 17 per cent within a year; average bus speeds inside the ring rose from 11 to 14 kilometres an hour; 61 million euros were collected in the first full year, of which 44 million went to extending two tram lines and the remainder funded an exemption scheme for residents inside the cordon; a bus route was withdrawn in 2019; and the tram extensions were not due to open until 2026.

provenance.notes: Original passage written for this item set. The city, the scheme and every figure in it are invented and internally consistent; nothing is quoted, adapted or summarised from any published article, report or test item. Questions built on it test reading of the passage only and never reward outside knowledge of any real congestion charge.
